speechtext: If hon. gentlemen will turn to the Votes and Proceedings of the 5th of May, they will find that I have given notice of an amendment to this Bill ?
What is the amendment ?

The amendment is as follows :
1.	Every railway company owning or operating a railway in the North-west Territories shall, on or before the thirty-first day of July in each year, provide a fire guard on each side of the line of railway upon any uncultivated or unoccupied land not covered each side by timber adjoining such railway, consisting of ploughed land at least eight feet in width which shall at all times thereafter during the year be kept free from grass and other inflammable matter.
2.	The fire guard shall be distant at least three hundred feet from the centre line of the railway, and the company shrill cause the grass to be burned off between it and such centre line not later than the first day of August in each year.
3.	The company shall, when causing such grass to be burned, have present sufficient persons and appliances to prevent the fire from spreading.
2.	Any company neglecting or failing to comply with any of the provisions of the foregoing section, and the officers and directors thereof, shall be liable, on summary conviction, to a penalty of $1,000 for each day of such neglect.
3.	For the purpose of complying with the provisions of section 1 hereof the company may enter upon any land not owned by it, and no claim for damages shall be maintained against the company for any act done in compliance with the provisions of the said section 1.
4.	This Act shall be read and construed as if it formed part of The Railway Act, chapter 23 of the statutes of 1888.
As is very clearly and plainly set out in that amendment, it is intended to compel railway companies operating lines in the North-west Territories to construct such fire guards as will prevent the spread of fires and the starting of what are known as prairie fires. To show the necessity for such action by parliament, I may state that within the last year there have been a number of very serious fires started from railway 144}
engines in the ranching country. Last fall one fire was started from the Calgary and Edmonton line, some distance north from Calgary, which burned what are known as the Nose creek and Beaver dam ranges That fire destroyed some 10,000 tons of hay and burned the houses and holdings of two settlers. East of Calgary last fall there were two very bad fires which burned over a large portion of the range country. East of Medicine Hat, too, there was a serious fire started from the railway which burned over the larger portion of the Cypress Hills country, and destroyed a very large quantity of hay which was put up for winter feed by the ranchers. South of the Bow river, south of Calgary, the most serious fires of the year occurred. Besides destroying the grass on a large area of the range, and burning a quantity of hay, it destroyed no less than 500 head of stock. We have spent a considerable time this session in discussing the want of cattle guards which seems to be a grievance in Ontario ; but 1 would venture to say that one single prairie fire in the range country will do as much damage as is done in four or five years through the lack of cattle guards. Within the past month there has been a series of serious fires started from the railway line, and I will take the liberty of reading a portion of a letter which came to me a few days ago from Medicine Hat, and which will give some information on this subject. It is dated April 13th, and the writer says : Since the 5th instant this country has been nearly ruined by prairie fires. On Saturday, the 5th instaut, a train leaving Medicine Hat set fire to the country on the west side of the river, and completely burnt over all the country north of the railway to the Red Deer river. The Canada Land and Ranch Company's farm at Stair, eight miles from Medicine Hat, is completely burnt over, not an acre left, and three fine Clyde mares are lying dead in their pasture burnt, and their fine herd of Galloway cattle are scattered all over the burnt country. On Tuesday a fire started on the railway somewhere near Dunmore, east of Medicine Hat, and has burnt the whole country clear to Swift Cur * rent. The Drowning Ford Ranch Company lost 300 tons of hay, and Charles Strong, rancher, of Walsh, lost all his hay, buildings, wagons and machinery, hay press, &c., and the loss to the stock industry will he very severe. The hay grounds are all hurnt over and will be no good for a couple of years. There have also been great fires in Alberta.
I may say to the committee that this matter was discussed in this House ten or eleven years ago. My late predecessor from Western Assiniboia brought the subject up in 1890 by way of resolution, very nearly in the terms of the amendment which I propose to-day. The resolution was discussed at length, and the government of that day accepted the spirit of it. The next year the same gentleman brought in a Bill in almost the identical terms of the present amendment. The principle of the measure was endorsed, and the Bill was read a second time; but I understand that at that

time the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, which was then the only railway company affected, agreed with the government that they recognized the need of action, and agreed that they would take action, and from that time to this the railway company have been doing considerable and expending considerable money in the way of fire-guarding their line. But the truth that they have not been attending to the matter completely is shown in the fact that this large number of serious fires have occurred and are occurring yearly. I may tell the committee, too, that if the railway company were subject to the control of the North-west assembly, there would be no need of action by this parliament. Every person in the North-west who is subject to the control of the assembly is liable to severe penalties for doing anything which may cause injury to the public by prairie fires. I may read the section of the prairie fire ordinance of the North-west assembly :
No person shall directly or indirectly, personally or by any servant, agent, or employee lilndle on any land a fire for the purpose of guarding property, burning stubble or brush or clearing land unless the land on which the fire is started is at the time It is started, completely surrounded by a fire guard not less than t\\ enty feet In width consisting of land covered with snow or water or so worn, graded, ploughed, burned over or covered with water as to be free of inflammable matter, and any person kindling a fire for such purpose shall during the whole oeriod of Its continuance cause it to be guarded by three adult persons provided with proper appliances for extinguishing prairie fire.
I think it is only right that a railway corporation should be subject to tbe same law in respect to this matter as are private individuals in that country. I think it is not right to allow a railway company or any corporation or any individual to carry an engine which results in destruction to property without having proper provision made to guard against the destruction. I beg, therefore, to move the adoption of this amendment.

I think the committee can hardly exaggerate the importance of the matter which my hon. friend from West Assiniboia (Mi-. Scott) has brought to our attention. It is a subject which has eugaged my attention at different times and in different ways, and I can, without any qualification, corroborate the statements he has made as to the very great damage which arises from these fires and as to the grievous consequences which follow, in some cases, to individuals who are wholly unable to bear the losses which they are called upon to bear. I have not followed the legal decisions on this subject within tbe last two or three years, but when last my attention was drawn to the details of the matter, my recollection is that, as the law stood, the railway company was not liable for a loss

by fire caused to an individual unless the person claiming damages could show that the railway company had been guilty of negligence. If the railway company could show that it had used the latest and best appliances known to science for the purpose of preventing the spread of fire, the best kind of spark arrester known, then it was held that the railway company was not guilty of negligence, and the person whose property was destroyed had no redress. I myself have known grievous cases in which fires caused by passing railway trains have burned wheat stacks, hay stacks, barns and houses of men who had absolutely nothing in tbe world besides what had been destroyed, and who could obtain no redress. If it were necessary to decide tbe point. I would not hesitate to say that if the state of knowledge in regard to the management of locomotives is such at tbe present time that it is not possible to prevent an occasional fire, wbicli results in the destruction of a large amount of private property, the House could well decide that the railway company could better afford to bear tbe loss, or a considerable portion of it, than the individual who has no means of protecting himself, who has not been guilty of any contributory negligence, but who, conducting his farming operations legally and properly on his own property, has liis property wiped out and destroyed.
My hon. friend has not however made any proposition which would tend to change the liability of a railway company in respect of tbe loss or destruction of property by fire, but has made a proposition which seems eminently reasonable and proper. It is that tbe railway companies, in that district of country, which is peculiarly liable to prairie fires, which run in such a way that once they get started they are almost inextinguishable. should take the necessary precautions for the purpose of preventing, as far as human foresight can do so. the spreading of these fires. When my hon. friend first spoke to me, in the early part of the session, about the proposition he now makes, I ventured the opinion that in all probability the cost would be enormous and almost prohibitory. But my hon. friend has made inquiries on that point, and he now informs me that the calculation which has been made, as the result of negotiations with the North-west Territorial government, results in the conclusion that the total expenditure by the Canadian Pacific Railway would be something in the neighbourhood of .$20,000. So far as I am personally concerned, I have not the least hesitation in saying that if over several hundred miles of railway running through such a country, by an expenditure of $20,000. life and property can be protected from danger of fire, it is the duty of the committee to impose on that company the obligation of providing that protection. But I think that my hon. friend will require to include the whole prairie country in his amendment, both Manitoba and the North-

west Territories. I think also that some of the latter portion of the amendment might well be left out, because it is probably covered by the general provisions of the Railway Act. Probably my hon. friend the Minister of Railways can speak on that point. But in so far as the general principle is concerned. I am entirely in favour of the amendment, though I am not ns a rule disposed to place any undue restrictions or obligations on any transportation company, which could have no practical result, simply for the furtherance of an idea. Having lived in that country since the Canadian Pacific Railway was incorporated, and before the first mile was constructed, I know that it is impossible to exaggerate the importance of the question which my hon. friend has brought to our attention. It has reference to a real and substantial grievance which this House ought to remedy.

(Translation.) I do not think the amendment moved by the hon. member for West Assiniboia goes far enough. By the clause which he wishes to embody in this Bill, the promoter deals only with the interests of the west, whereas the Bill under discussion concerns the country at large.
In the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company vs. Roy, the Judiciary Committee of the Privy Council has decided that a railway company which, in running its railway, complies with all the requirements of its charter, is not liable for damages ensuing from fire arising from the sparks emitted from any locomotive engine, in the normal use of its line. That you should use your own property so as not to injure your neighbour's property, is a principle of Roman law embodied in the legislation of every civilized country.
A company has the right to the normal use of its property, but it cannot go beyond that. When a company, in rufining its railway, sets fire to the neighbouring property, it goes beyond the lawful and normal [DOT] use of its property, and it trespasses upon foreign ground. The Judiciary Committee of the Privy Council did not hold that it was not fair and just that a railway company should not be liable for damages resulting from the use of its line ; on the contrary, the law lords held that it was common law, but they decided that a railway company was above common law, under the power conferred upon it by its federal charter. When the question was threshed out on the floor of the Quebec legislature, M. Duffy drew attention to that fact and spoke ns follows :
It is admitted that it is unjust that Roy should have had his property damaged by the railway company, even when that company was without fault. What is the remedy ?
The remedy does not consist in abolishing, all appeals to the Privy Council and of doing away with that learned body so far as this province is concerned. The privilege consists in calling
upon the Dominion parliament not to pass legislation where it has the jurisdiction which will permit such an injustice. A simple amendment to the Railway Act, providing that railways would be liable for damage caused in the manner mentioned in this case would- of course do away with the evil.
There is no doubt that a railway company cannot trespass upon private property. If in the course of its operations, a railway company sets fire to a property of a farmer, upon whom shall the loss fall ? It must fall either upon the railway company or the farmer who Is the victim. But it stands to reason that the railway company lias no right to the use of a property that does not belong to it. I beg therefore to move the following amendment:
Whenever damage is caused to crops, lands, fences, plantations, or' buildings, and their contents, by flres started by a railway locomotive, the company making use of such locomotive, shall, notwithstanding any provision in any general or special Act of the parliament of Canada, be responsible for such damage, and may be sued for the recovery of the amount of such damage in. any court of ordinary jurisdiction.

What the hon. gentleman proposes to do is to engraft an entirely new principle, so far as the larger portion of the Dominion of Canada is concerned, upon the liabilities of railway companies. He asks that parliament should uilirin, irrespective of Whether or not a railway company is guilty of negligence, and although the company may have conformed in every particular with the requirements of the law, although it may have adopted the most recent up to date method for the protection of property along its tracks, that if damage should ensue to property through the necessary and ordinary use of the railway, the railway company shall be liable to make good to the person suffering such damage, any amount necessary for such purpose. That possibly may be a wise provision to adopt as part of the general law of the land, but 1 think my hon. friend would hardly expect that in the dying hours of the session, when we can scarcely give the subject the attention and consideration it demands, we should subscribe to the adoption of a new principle and an entire change in the doctrines and principles of common law, as they now regulate the question of negligence. 1 would not like at this moment to say that the committee ought' to adopt this amendment, and I think perhaps the effect would be to complicate and injuriously affect whatever element there may 'be of merit in the amendment which the hon. member for West Assiniboia is asking ns to consider. The question which arises under the amendment of my hon. friend from West Assiniboia is one which must largely depend upon existing circumstances and upon the possibility of an adequate and sufficient remedy lying in the hands of the railway company.

and a remedy which would not necessarily entail extraordinary and unreasonable cost to the company. I am not going to say that a railway company should not, even at great expense, be required to protect properties in the district it traverses, but I do think it would have been better if we had been able to hear, before coming to a conclusion, the other parties who are interested, for instance, the railway companies, who might wish to have something to say on the subject. I agree with the hon. gentleman who has moved this amendment and the hon. minister who has supported it, that a very strong case possibly can be made out, but is it wise, though the grievance is a serious one, though enormous damage has resulted to the people by reason of sufficient safeguards not having been provided heretofore, for us, in this form and at this moment, to say that this is the only and proper way in which the needed protection shall be provided.
Personally, I would gladly respond to any appeal which might be made by the hon. gentleman for legislative action in the matter. But I would not like to commit myself to this method,, unless I had an opportunity to inform myself upon the subject, and should conclude that this was the best mode by which the remedy could be provided. I should imagine that, possibly, the meaning of this first clause would be that not only would the company have to Plough the land on either side of the track, but they might be obliged to continue ploughing it-two or three different ploughing might be required. The company might be obliged to keep constantly ploughing on either side of the track from the last of July for the rest of the season. Is that a necessary thing to do ? And, if so, can it reasonably be done ? I would go as far as any hon. gentleman in pressing upon the railway company the duty of providing a sufficient safeguard. The existing condition is a very serious one, no doubt, one for which a remedy should be found. But is this the only remedy, and are we providing for it in a proper way ?
I feel some uncertainty about the matter myself, and therefore would not like very ardently to accept the motion. But I would not oppose it without hearing the opinions of others. There is a section which provides a penalty of $1,000 for each day of neglect of this ploughing. That would mean, I presume, that this penalty would be enforcible against the railway company for neglect at any point over its entire line. If that is a correct Interpretation, still, if the first clause is one which meets with favour from the committee, I would not feel that the penalty was unduly severe. The third section provides :
For the purpose of complying with the provisions of cect on 1 hereof the company may enter upon any land not owned by it, and no claim, for damages shall be maintained against Hon. Mr. BLATR.
the company for any act done in compliance with the provisions of the said section 1.
Perhaps it is not necessary to regard that as a very serious question, though I mention it to call the attention of the committee to it. I confess to feeling a good deal of difficulty with regard to the proposed amendment. I would like to see something done. My hon. frieud (Mr. Scott) has not had-it is no fault of liis- the opportunity of having the matter presented and considered earlier. The fact that my hon. friend had given notice of this amendment was not brought to my attention until just before my motion for second reading 6f tbe Bill was made.. Therefore, I have not had-and perhaps other gentlemen are in the same position-the opportunity to consider the matter and reach a satisfactory conclusion in my own mind. But. if the sense of the committee it not averse to the proposition, I would not offer any objection.	_.
speakername: The MINISTER OE RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The fact that the hon. gentleman proposed the second amendment, the purpose of which is to deal with the points to which I adverted when I was on my feet a few moments ago, viz. : the liability of the company, shows that this is a question which has given rise to serious difficultv and serious consideration long before the present time, and not only so, but that the different methods of meeting the difficulty have been very carefully considered. Now, I submit that in so far as the method of meeting the difficulty with respect to the prairie country to which my bon. friend from West Assi-niboia's motion refers, is concerned, no simpler or less expensive method could possibly be devised than that suggested. We are simply acting on the maxim that prevention is better than cure-that preventing a fire is better than paying damages for tlie results of fire. And, if we are in a position to estimate the expense approximately, as my hon. friend from West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) is satisfied we are, . I do not think that the committee will regard $20,000 or even $50,000 as an excessive amount to call upon a railway company to expend in order to protect a vast territory of that kind against the destruction which comes yearly by the starting of prairie fires. In this proposal, then, we have it appears to me. a simple, practicable, and not oppressivley expensive, method of meeting the difficulty. I would urge upon the committee that the usual indisposition to deal with such matters at a late period of the session should not influence us in this ease. My hon. friend from West Assiniboia has been diligent enough in getting this matter before the House, and the fact that lie has not succeeded In bringing it before tbe House at an earlier time is due to no fault of his, but to circumstances over which be lias liad no control. But if

the matter were considered for six months, ( though the committee might have greater knowledge of the details, yet I doubt if it would be in a better position to deal with the matter than at the present time. As my hon. friend (Mr. Scott) has stated, this is a subject which has been discussed between the railway company and the North-west government, and the fact that it is practicable to carry out this plan, and that it is, to all intents and purposes effective, is practically admitted by all parties concerned. All that is necessary is for this parliament to place upon the railway company the obligation, which, I think, every lion, member here will admit should be placed upon them, of taking reasonable precautions to protect the public from the loss which has hitherto been suffered. Let the railway companies understand that parliament has placed this obligation upon them, and we shall have no more difficulty about prairie fires starting from locomotives. The railway companies would do what they have done in other cases, they would take the necessary steps to comply with the conditions, and parliament might feel that at least it had prevented very serious losses such as have taken place during the past years. To my own knowledge railway companies themselves have very fully appreciated the difficulties of this question, and, as long ago as seven or eight years,
I remember, the Canadian Pacific Railway made prolonged efforts to provide an inexpensive and effective means of clearing the fire-guard along its track. A complicated piece of machinery for that purpose was devised, but I believe it did not turn out successful in operation. As to the necessity of ploughing the fire-guards a second time, X think I can state to the Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair) that such a difficulty would not arise. If in the case of the virgin prairie, land is ploughed once between the 1st and the 31st of July, seed will not germinate in such a way as to make it necessary to plough that land again-there will be nothing inflammable there except what is blown upon it. If the provisions of the amendment are carried out, the fire-guard might be ploughed anywhere between the 1st of July and the 31st of July; then, the ground between the fire-guard and the track being cleared, it will form an effective fire-guard for the rest of that season. So that difficulty as a matter of actual practice will not apply. The same thing might be said of a fire-guard being applied where the land had been cultivated before. Seeds will not germinate in such a way as to place any inflammable matter upon the ground which is ploughed after the 1st of July of any season. So we may, I think, feel satisfied that the amendment is an effective one, that it will accomplish the purpose for which it is designed, that it is not unreasonably oppressive, and that it
is actually necessary for the purpose of removing a substantial grievance.

In my opinion the the amendment moved by the hon. member for St. Johu's (Mr. Demers) will have the effect of changing the law altogether as it at present exists in Canada and in Great Britain. The law, I think, was very properly laid down by the Minister of the Interior when he said that a railroad company receiving a charter or a right to run through a country, when it exercises due precaution in running and is not guilty of negligence, is not liable to these incidental damages. The hon. member for St. John's would make the companies liable for the incidence, even the damage resulted after the use of the utmost diligence on the part of the company, and the utmost precaution in running the road. That is contrary to the principle of the law of this country, it is contrary to the law laid down in Great Britain ; and it is contrary, if I understand properly the decision of the Privy Council of England the other day, to the code in Quebec. Notwithstanding the decision of the courts in Quebec on the matter, the Privy Council in England found that their interpretation of the code was wrong, and that the law was similar to what it is in our section of the country. It would be an entire reversal of the law as at present applied to railroads both in this country, in Great Britain and in the United States. However, I do not suppose there is any chance of it becoming law at this session, as I am glad to hear from the remarks of the Minister of the Interior that it was not his intention to press the amendment in reference to fire guards at the present session.
My hon. friend must have misunderstood me. What I said was that I would press the committee to adopt it.

The hon. gentleman advocated it, and complimented his hon. friend on the introduction of the amendment, but the inference I drew from the remarks of the Minister of the Interior was that on account of the late period of the session it could not be fully discussed and considered at the present time. However, I state my objection to the section. I think the railroad companies in the North-west already try to protect, not only their own property by running ploughed tracks along their line, but also the property of the farmers in the neighbourhood. I do not know whether they are compelled to do it, or whether the territories have power to Compel them to do it ; I do not know whether it is in accordance with the North-west Act. But the question I want to present to this House is whether we have power to legislate in this direction ? Is it an incidence to railroad travelling or railroad chartering ?
* 4591

I think so.
Hon. Mr. HAGGAR l'. I have a (liltevent opinion. We may make anything an incidence that we like in reference to railroads, we may say that they shall not run a railway unless they do so and so. But surely we have no power to pass a clause like this for the purpose of making them comply with all the provisions of section 1, which reads :
The company roav enter upon any land not owned by it, and no claim for damages shall be maintained against the company for any act done ir. compliance with the provisions of said section.
What is the object of the hon. gentleman in Introducing his amendment ? It is to protect the farms in the neighbourhood of the railways from damage done by fire. It is not an incidence to the running of the road that they should exercise due precaution ; it is not within our power to give them the right to enter on private property and take possession of it for the purpose of doing or preventing a damage by fire to farms in the neighbourhood.
The MINISTER OF RAILWAlS AND CANALS. Would we not require them to keep their track in a certain condition ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: We could require them to keep their track in a good condition, we could require them to exercise due precaution against fire ; but we could not give them power to enter upon private property and take possession of it, without compensation, for the purpose of preventing fire spreading to neighbouring farms.

The question of compensation is a question for parliament. It is within our discretion. We can authorize the railway companies to do anything we consider necessary for the due protection of the public, either in regard to travelling upon the railway or in regard to traffic. Anything in the judgment of this parliament that is necessary for the protection of the public we can enact, and we can place that obligation upon the railway company.

This is not for me protection of the public, this is not for the protection of traffic. It is not an incidence to the exercise by a railway corporation of its rights and powers. This is for the protection of farmers in the neighbourhood of a railway from damage done, though not through the negligence of the company.
We require the railway company to do a particular thing, and when they do not do it, then they become negligent, and being negligent, they are liable for damages when that negligence is established.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: You may put any obligation on a railway company that you like. Y'ou may define what is an incidence to it, and what is negligence ; but can you give them power to exercise the right of going on to the property of a private individual without compensation, and doing what you wish them to do ?
If it is necessary for the purpose of the Act.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Not at all. The clause reads :
For the purpose of complying with the provisions of section 1, hereinafter, the company nay enter upon any land not owned by it, and no claim for damages shall be maintained against the company for any act done in compliance with the provisions of said section.
You may say that the company may be negligent in doing anything, you may make any condition that you like in giving them their charter ; but you caunot interfere with provincial rights, you cannot say they shall enter upon any man's property for the purpose of doing something which is not an incidence to railroad traffic. But there ig another objection still more serious which I wish to mention. The railway companies ought to have a right to state their case, either before parliament or a committee of parliament. 'Who is to determine whether the protection is proper, or whether a certain act is necessary to afford protection? Therefore I think the hou. gentleman who introduced this section will perform his duty to his constituents if he lets the amendment stand as a notice, and let the railway companies be beard in reference to these amendments. Amendments like this affect large amounts of capital which have been invested in this country. The parties should be heard before a committee of the House. It is unfair to the railway companies to enact legislation of this kind without their being heard before some authority appointed by this House for the purpose.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think there is any desire on the part of the hon. member (Mr. Scott) to be unfair to the railway companies, or to take the House unawares in any way. I understand that the hon. member has made every effort to get his Bill before the House, and that he did make every effort to get his Bill before the House at an earlier date in the session. Owing to circumstances he was not able to do so, and it is now for the House to say whether it considers it has received suifi-eient information on the subject to warrant it in coming to a conclusion or postponing that conclusion to some future occasion.
I would like to say, however, iu reply to the contention set up by the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Haggart), that parliament is here for the purpose of discussing and deciding these questions oil

its own responsibility, and it is not absolutely necessary to tbe decision of the question that the private parties to the case shall be heard by parliament. Parliament is responsible for the decision, parliament can arrive at the decision by any means Its sees fit, and it is not compelled to wait for such evidence as would be given before a court of law before reaching its conclusion.
In regard to the general question, there seems to be a very grave misapprehension on the part of lion, members as to what is attempted to be done. It is essentially not a question of protecting the farmers or farming property. It is an absolutely and entirely different question from the question brought forward by the hon. member for St. John and Iberville (Mr. Demers). It is a question rather of protecting public property than of protecting private property. The country owns the laud, the country owns the grass, the country derives a benefit from the use of that grass by reason of it being pastured by cattle and turned into valuable beef. It is in regard to tbe range country rather than in regard -to the farming country that these amendments are suggested, and in regard to which the question chiefly arises. We have a condition of affairs that Is absolutely different from that prevailing in any other part of the Dominion, and hon. members may be forgiven for not accurately understanding that position. It is because tbe condition is so radically different there from the condition elsewhere in the Dominion that we are asking for such radically different legislation. It is a different case, and therefore, we are asking for different legislation.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question ?
Yes.
In the western states [DOT]they have very much the same conditions as we have on this side. Is the hon. gentleman aware of what means they take to check the spread of fires on the ranges ?

I have not the faintest idea, but there is another piece of information which I will give to the hon. gentleman, and it is that in the range country of the western states the grass is not as rank, it is not as good as it is in the Northwest, and therefore it is not as subject to the spread of prairie fires. The grass, being longer in our country, when i't becomes dry, the fire is much more easily and much more certainly spreads upon it.
The grass, as I say, belongs to tbe country. The country derives benefit from that grass, either directly toy rental, or indirectly by the production of wealth in the growth of beef, and it is with the view of protecting the public interest, or the national interest, in that property, raither than protecting the private interest of the individual, that this
amendment is proposed. Because, in the vast areas of country which have been burned over year after year by fires started by Canadian Pacific Railway locomotives, a very small proportion of (the country lias become private property, while a very large proportion of it is producing actual wealth fo.r the country. The greater part of the area affected is not private property, it is public property, and parliament lias a perfect right to direct that any action shall be taken lii regard to that property that parliament desires. But, of course, a large part of the range country is also private property. It is owned, and in some cases, it is fenced. But there is no distinction in appearance, or in use, there is not even a boundary set up in many cases between what is private property and what is public property, and I can assure tlie committee that the fire does not recognize any difference between private and jniblic property, between land that is owned and land that is not owned. If a fire starts on private property it spreads to the public domain, and if it starts on the public domain it overwhelms private property. It is a case in which the private and the public interest is the same. They are identical, the one has to toe protected with' the other, and the one cannot be protected without the other. There is no use requiring a railway company to go on public property and plough fire-guards and not require them to go on private property and plough fireguards.
As to the constitutional question, or the question of law that has been raised, I will say nothing, but I will ask the committee if it seems good to nllow this vast interest that exists in our country, that Is increasing in value from year to year, to be jeopardized because of a constitutional point, because of some question in law, because of a ruling made by a judge on a question that does not appertain in any shape or manner to the condition of affairs which exists in these territories at the present time. What I ask the committee to do is to take into consideration the fact that the conditions are as they are. that they are absolutely and entirely different from any conditions existing in any of the eastern provinces, that it is the public interest that requires protection, that it cannot be protected separately from the private interest, that common cause lias to be made against the common enemy, that is fire, that the local legislature has no authority in the matter, that .this Dominion parliament is the only authority, and that, as far as our judgment goes-I speak of the western members-we have not been able to suggest any better remedy for meeting wliat is a tremendous and a growing evil than the suggestion made by the hon. member for West Assiutboia (Mr. Scott).

It would probably lie well for ime to give the committee the fullest information I can as to how this provision

would work out in practice if it is enacted. The only company, which, to-day, would he affected, is the Canadian Pacific Railway.
And the Canadian Northern.

The Canadian Northern has only a few miles of road in the territories, and the class of country in which they are at present is such that they would not require to observe this provision. I will give the committee the total mileage of the Canadian Pacific Railway which would be affected. On the main line guarding would be necessary between Qu'Appelle and Morley, 558 miles. There would be a mileage of 100 miles on the Soo branch, 1G0 miles on the Prince Albert branch, 165 miles on the Calgary and Edmonton branch and 211 miles on the Crow's Nest Pass Railway, making a total mileage of 1,254 miles. That mileage, of course, has to be doubled for guarding is necessary on both sides of the line, so that it makes practically 2,500 miles.
Do they not do something in that direction now ?
They do a very considerable amount.
Are the railway company complying as far as possible with the territorial law in this particular ?

The territorial legislature are not competent to control the company in this matter. If the legislature were competent to do so I can assure my hon. friend that no action would need to be suggested in this parliament. I have the figures which have been prepared by I believe the most competent authority in the North-west Territories, the most competent person in Canada, with respect to this matter and he calculates that the cost of the first construction of such a guard would be about $10 per mile, amounting to $25,000 over the whole system. That would be in the first year, and he also calculates that the cost of maintenance in subsequent years would be $5 a mile for the back setting or re-breaking of the ploughed guard and about $3 a mile for the burning between the ploughed guard and the railway track. I may say to my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals that the ploughed guard is not the chief thing, the burning between the guards and the track is the chief thing, and if that is done completely once a year it will be entirely sufficient. The total cost of maintenance therefore would be about .$8 per mile, or as the Minister of the Interior has already said, a total of $20,000 per year. The hon. gentleman (Mr. I-Iaggart) has suggested that the company is already doing considerable in this direction, and that being the case we will not by this amendment be imposing a burden of $20,000 a year upon this company. I have no doubt that the company is already expending

possibly $10,000 or $12,000 a year, so that this amendment would not impose a very great additional burden upon them. The fact that the company is not completely fire-guarding its system is proven by the very many and very serious fires which have occurred last fall and this spring.
Now, as to the feasibility of the particular plan which is suggested, I may say that the Public Works Department of the Northwest government and the railway company have been negotiating with respect to this matter for two or three years, and the plan which they have decided on as being the best is exactly this plan which I have now proposed. The North-west government deemed the matter so very important in the public interest that, although they did not believe the government should be saddled with any portion of the cost, yet they went the length of suggesting that they would bear a portion of the cost if the railway company would undertake to complete the fire-guarding of their system. The company and the government are entirely agreed that this plan which is here suggested is the best plan, is a good plan, but they did not arrive at an agreement as to the terms. I understand that the government went the length of suggesting that they would be willing to bear half of the whole cost of first construction and maintenance, but so far as I have been informed the railway company did not see fit to agree to even that proposition.
Respecting the sub-clause which would give the company power to go upon other people's property without compensation, I may say that in practice 1 do not think any difficulty will be found. When the railway company were willing to agree with the North-west government to carry out this particular plan, they did not think evidently that there would be any serious difficulty encountered in that respect. In the portion of the country which is a farming country this fire-guard is not necessary, and it is only in the ranching country where people live far apart that it will have to be constructed. The people living in such a section are not likely to object to the company going upon their property, but as it would seem unreasonable to make a law compelling the company to do certain things and not relieve them from liability for damage for so doing, we have inserted this clause in the amendment. I draw the attention of the House to the fact that the proposition w'hich we make with respect to prairie fires in the North-west is entirely on all fours with the proposition which was agreed to by a majority of the members of this House and by the government on the cattle-guard question. It was decided in that case that it would be better to find out what is the best cattle-guard and then to compel the railway companies to use that cattle-guard subject to a penalty for neglecting the use of it. I claim that I am suggesting

to-day what is the best fire-guard, and I ask parliament to compel the railway companies to use that fire-guard subject to a penalty for failing to do so.

This is a very important question, and although I think it would be fair that the railway company should have an opportunity of presenting their view, yet that cannot be done during this session at least. I have some knowledge of the injury that has been done not only in the Northwest but in Ontario because of fires started by railway engines, and I confess that I would be inclined to go the length of saying that the railway company should not only be obliged to take precautions to prevent tires starting, but that they should be held responsible as well for damages done in this connection. In my own locality I have seen a fanner burned out three or four times ova- by reason of fire starting from railway engines, and yet he was unable to get a dollar of compensation. That is not justice. If a farmer lights a fire to clean his land after the 1st of June, and damage results from that fire, the law provides that he shall be responsible. Why should you impose such liability upon a private individual and exempt a great railway corporation. That is something that I cannot understand. If the information which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) gives us is correct, then the adoption of this amendment would not impose any very great expense upon the railway companies. He tells us that they would have to plough a section of the country sixteen feet wide and 1,272 miles long. That would be in all 3,544 acres, and assuming that it would cost 81.50 an acre-it would only have to be ploughed once in a season, although perhaps there might be localities where it would be necessary to plow more than once-but if done once in the season it would give fairly good protection and it would cost the railway company only $5,316. It happens very frequently that one farmer sustains a loss from these railway fires more than three times that amount, not considering the thousands of acres of pasture which are burned and the consequent heavy loss to cattle owners whose feed for their cattle has been destroyed.
Comparatively speaking it would be a very small expense to a rich corporation ; but when you take into account the loss sustained by individuals and their helplessness under the circumstances, our sympathy should go to the individual rather than to the rich corporation. For this reason I would be inclined to support the amendment. I am not sufficiently versed in law to be able to say whether there is anything in the constitutional point raised by the hon. member for South Lanark ; but assuming that we have the authority to legislate, the question is. should we put that obligation upon the railway companies ? In my judgment we should. We give these corporations great powers and privileges. We give them franchises out of which they are able to earn immense amounts of money from the people. We give them rights which they exercise over the people, very often to the detriment and loss of private individuals. In almost every instance in which the interests of individuals are concerned, these suffer instead of the railway. In consideration of these things, I do not think it is too much to put upon the railways the obligation to bear the consequences of the damage they do. While I admit that the railway companies ought to be heard. I do not admit that we are not justified in passing this amendment, because I think we are. I, for one, would be inclined to go further, and say that we should, hold them responsible for all the damage done by their locomotives, not only in Manitoba, but in every other part of the country. In carrying on ordinary business, if we do damage to another, we must pay for that damage ; and I do not see why a railway company should not be compelled to do that which a private individual must do.
Mr. BELCOi ilT. I quite agree with the hon. gentleman who has preceded me as to the importance of this question. I regret that I am not in a position to speak to the House very intelligently upon it. because I did not see or hear of the amendment until it was read this afternoon ; but I may say that I have for some time made up my mind on this question. I quite agree with the hon. gentleman who lias just sat down that the legislation aimed at in the amendment proposed by the hon. member for St. Johns and Iberville (Mr. Demers) is right, and expedient for this parliament to enact. Until the Privy Council decided recently the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway vs. Roy. I had thought that the provision of section 288 of the Railway Act (1888) had consecrated the principle embodied in this amendment ; but the Privy Council has declared the principle to be non-existent in Canada. With the permission of the House I will read section 288 :
No inspection had under this Act, r.nd nothing in this Act contained, and nothing done or ordered or omitted to be done or ordered, under or by virtue of the provisions of this Act, shall relieve, or he construed to relieve, any company, of or from any liability or resnonsibility resting upon it by law, either towirds Her Majesty cr towards any person, or the wife or husband, parent or child, executor or administrator, tutor or curator, heir or personal representative of any person, for anything done or omitted to be done by such company, or for any wrongful act, neglect or default, misfeasance, malfeasance or nonfeasance, of such company or in any manner or way to lessen such liability or responsibility, or in any way to weaken or diminish the liability or responsibility of any such company, under the laws in force In the province in which such liability or responsibility arises.

I liad always been under the impression that tins section preserved and sanctioned tlie principle that corporations or individuals who exercise an occupation or carry on a trade or occupation which is of a dangerous or obnoxious character, when that is done for gain or profit, do so at their own risk, and if in doing so they cause damage to any person, whatever precautions they take, they are liable for that damage. I have always thought that section 288 consecrated that principle ; but it is evident that I was wrong If the recent decision of the Privy Council is the true interpretation of the law. I would not venture to say, whatever my opinion is, that the decision of the Privy Council is wrong. But, I think. I may say that it has been guided more by the principles of English law than by the principle I have mentioned is recognized by the French law, and runs all through French jurisprudence. It may be that it has not received full sanction in regard to the railways of France ; but that is explained by the" fact that the railways of France are mostly owned and managed by the state, and that the state has thought it well to protect itself from damages arising from fire on the ground that it does not operate the railways for profit or gain. Therefore the principle which permeates the whole of French legislation, has not received in France with regard to railways the sanction 'that it has received with regard to other subjects. I think the amendment of my hon. friend all the more expedient because of the interpretation which section 288 has been given by the Privy Council. It seems to me the amendment is not only expedient, but right and just. What are the facts ? A company is created by parliament for the purpose of carrying on the business of a public carrier. It is given certain powers which it can exercise, but if in the exercise of those powers it causes any damage to the people along its line, it seems to me the company ought to pay that damage. It is well enough to say that this parliament is supreme, and that it can enact any law. Of course it can; it can pass an unjust or iniquitous law. I am not discussing what this parliament can do ; I am discussing what it ought to do in a case of this sort. It is said that the course of legislation in England has been different from what is proposed here. I do not say that it has ; but assuming that it has, it does not follow that we must go on for ever bound by legislation which perpetrates an injustice. When this country was new and the means of communication were difficult, it was probably just that every facility should be given to railway companies to carry on their business ; but that time is past, and we have to-day railways passing through very thickly populated sections of the country, among hundreds of thousands of people whose property is daily and hourly subject to fire. The principle for which I contend has been sanctioned in the matter of expro-Mr. BELCOURT.
priation. It is true, this parliament has given power to railway companies to expropriate property from individuals for the purposes of the railway ; but parliament has imposed restrictions and a procedure under which th:ft must be done, and has also taken care to provide that in giving compensation to the people whose property is expropriated, the railway company must take certain matters into account.
It seems to me that this proposed legislation is eminently proper and just. Here is a railway company, which operates a dangerous undertaking for its own profit and advantage. Why should the people who live along the line of that railway be subject, not only to the noise, smoke and vibration and other inconvenience arising from it, but also to damages caused by fire. The principle for which I contend has been admitted in almost every other case where a dangerous or obnoxious trade or business is carried on. Our courts have frequently decided that persons operating a saw mill in a city should pay damages caused by the vibration of its machinery or by the smoke emanating from it. In a recent case in the city of Montreal, a livery stable keeper was condemned to pay the damages caused his neighbour's property by the bad smell emanating from his stable. The principle is not a new one, and I see no reason why railway companies should not be subjected to it as well as every other kind of business. The argument that the time has come for a change in our legislation in this regard is not a new one. In the imperial parliament in 1900, a Bill was introduced which is substantially to the same effect as the proposed amendment. That Bill provided as follows :
Where damages caused to crops, hedges, or plantations by Are arising from sparks emitted from any locomotive engine on railways, the railway company owning such engine shall, notwithstanding their statutory powers and rights to the contrary, or the provisiois of any special or general Act relating thereto, he liable to pay to the person whose crops, hedges, or plantations have been so damaged, the amount of such damage to he recovered iu any court of competent jurisdiction.
That is botli law and justice.

That Bill did not pass, but there was a majority of practically four to one in its favour, the vote on second reading, I am toldf standing 330 for and 84 against.
Similar legislation exists also in many states of the American Union. It seems to me that the time has come when we should compel railway companies to pay the damages they cause. The argument that these companies are operating pro bono publico is altogether exploded. The Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway and the other railway companies are not carrying on their business for the benefit of tlie public, but for the dollars and

cents they can make ont of it, and I cannot see why a poor farmer, whose lands are often cut in two by these railway lines, should, besides having to run the danger of crossing the railway track in the operations of his farm, be also subjected, besides many other inconveniences and annoyances, to loss by fire caused by the sparks from locomotives. I do not delude myself into the belief that the House will adopt this resolution to-day when parliament is on the eve of prorogation, for I am afraid that a number of hon. members are not quite so zealous in the matter as are my hon. friend from St. .Tean d'Iberville (Air. Demers) and myself, and many others, but I believe that those who are in fovour of this proposed legislation should put themselves on record and thus create a public opinion that will eventually bring about its adoption.
The PRIAIB All MISTER. Personally 1 am in sympathy with both amendments, especially that introduced by my hon. friend from St. Jean d'Iberville (Mr. Demers). If that amendment were adopted, we would have legislation on our statute books, which would not only be law but also equity. I cannot conceive of any reasonable argument against such a law. A company is authorized to carry on a certain enteiprise, and at present, if it makes use of the latest inventions for protection against damage, it is n<5t responsible. That may be law, but it is not equity. If in the course of its operations, a railway company sets fire to a poor man's crop, as often happens, the company pleads that as it has taken all the precautions possible, it is not responsible for any loss. The company pleads that the loss occurred through no fault of its own. That may be, but neither was it the fault of the poor man whose property was destroyed. A loss has to be borne; upon whom shall it fall. It must fall either upon the railway company or the settler, who is the victim, and under the circumstances certainly equity demands that the victim should not suffer the damage, but the party who caused it, even though that party be free of blame. For my part I am in favour of the amendment of my hon. friend from St. Jean d'Iberville, and I am also much in sympathy with that of my hon. friend from West Ass'niboia, although the latter amendment is not free from doubt. There is a good deal to be said in favour of the argument of the hon. member for Lanark (Air. Haggart). I do not know that we have the power at this moment, though we might have had it when granting the charter, to provide that a company shall be authorized to go on private property and there put up any construction it may deem necessary. I would ask both my hon. friends not to press their amendments, not because I am not in favour of them, but because I think it would be wiser to follow the usual method of dealing with such matters. Aly hon. friend
from Alberta (Air. Oliver) has said that parliament should deal with these questions as it pleases. That is no doubt true, but parliament has thought fit to adopt certain rules, and it is always better to follow these rules, even when we nave made up our minds that there is no other side to the question. But there are two sides to every question, and It is only right that we should give the railway companies an opportunity of presenting their views before enacting any legislation of the kind proposed. The rule hitherto followed is that legislation of this kind should be referred to the Railway Committee, where opportunity is given to all parties to bring witnesses and have the whole question properly threshed out. I would suggest that that rule be followed in this case, and I would say to my hon. friends from West Assiniboia and St. Jean D'Iberville, that the government pledges itself to give them an opportunity early next session to have this matter referred to the Railway Committee in order tbirt it may be discussed there in all its phases, and proper legislation drafted. With this assurance, I hope that my hon. friends will agree to follow the course I have suggested.

There is one thing I would like to say, and that is that while this evil may be greater in the Northwest than in other parts of Canada, it is by no means confined to that particulhr part of the country. In the eastern provinces we have had many cases in which property has been destroyed by fire from locomotive engines, and the parties interested have been unable to recover because they could not show negligence on the part of the railway company. In other words, a railway company is not liable so long as it is shown that it has employed the latest and most improved methods known to science for the purpose of preventing fire being communicated to the adjoining property. When this question comes to be discussed next year, as the right hon. gentleman says it will be, there is one subject which the government should consider in that connection, and that is the liability of the Crown by reason of its operation of the Intercolonial Railway. There is no special reason why the Intercolonial Railway should not be subject to the same rules as other railways in that regard. It runs through a large portion of Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, and at present I do not see what remedy there is, in case of damage, even if negligence were established. I know that there is a statute which says that the Crown is liable for negligence committed by any of its servants on public works, but whether or not that would apply to the case of the user by the Crown of a locomotive not	in conformity
with the latest	improvements, is a
question I have not looked into.

When the government come to deal with this question in the North-west, I think they will perhaps he obliged to deal with it on different lines from those on which it should be dealt with in the other provinces. I suppose that a provision of the character suggested by the hon. member for West Assiniboia would not be of very much use in the older provinces. Therefore, I think that when the question presents itself to the government next year it will probably present itself in the somewhat broader aspect than that in which it is presented in the amendments of my hon. friend from West Assiniboia-more in the light of the amendment introduced by my hon. friend from St. John and Iberville. It is a pretty large question. Railway companies have been exempt from liability in the past by reason of the fact that they operate their railways under laws which empower them to do so, and which, for the most part, provide that their lines shall be located in certain places. This was the cause of exemption in the first place, the reason why they were exempt from being treated as a public nuisance. They were authorized by statute, or by ordinance having the force of law, to operate their lines in particular places. But that does not apply to all corporations carrying on business. A great deal depends on the terms of the particular statutes. It is a great question in this [DOT]country, particularly in view of the fact that great industrial enterprises are being advanced at the present time. You must consider not only ithe liabilities of railway companies carrying on enterprises of that character, but you must* consider the liability that should attach to other corporations, such as the great manufacturing concerns. It is a subject that is by no means free from difficulty and will involve a great deal of debate. The question with which we are more immediately concerned is the liability of the railway companies. As far as they are concerned, ithere seemsi a great deal of force in what has been urged from both sides that persons who, through no fault of tlieir own, have property destroyed through the causes we have been discussing, should have some remedy pointed out to them, or, at all events, (those exposed to such danger should have, possibly some better safeguard employed than is at present provided. But I entirely agree with what has been said by the right hon. leader of the House as to the unwisdom of dealing with ithis question without giving the railway companies an opportunity to put the other side of the question. It may be that there is no other side to the question-the Minister of the Interior says that there is not. That is all very well, but the railway companies should be heard from, and, after hearing we can judge better whether there is another side to the question or not. It is true that in questions of this kind this parliament is paramount. I believe that parliament lias power to pass this legisla-

tion. But parliament should not, without hearing the other side, always exercise the power it possesses. Otherwise a local legislature, having jurisdiction over property and civil rights, could pass one man's property over to any other without giving the man whose property was being sacrificed the opportunity of saying a word in his own defence. That might be the result of the argument presented by my hou. friend from Alberta (Mr. Oliver) if carried out to its legitimate conclusion. I think it is quite right to postpone this legislation to another session, and, when it conies up again it should foe discussed from all standpoints, and after hearing nil parties interested.

So far as concerns the amendment that I proposed, I desire to say that it is with very extreme regret I feel impelled by the remarks which have been made by the right hon. leader of the House (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) to ask permission to withdraw it.
Amendment, (Mr. Scott), withdrawn.

I also beg leave to withdraw the amendment I offered.
Amendment, (Mr. Demers), withdrawn.
Bill reported.
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS moved the third reading of the Bill.

Before the Bill is read the third time, I would ask the hou. gentleman (Mr. Blair) what is the explanation of the words to which I called attention this morning. Is the effect of the section this-that the person whose land is taken for this temporary purpose shall have notice of what land is taken, and will he have compensation, and will he have the usual remedy ?

He is entitled to compensation, and he will have the usual remedy provided in the original statute.
Motion agreed to; Bill read the third time, and passed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Bill (No. 164) to amend the Act of 1S09 respecting the city of Ottawa (the Minister of Finance) was read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,
Do the commissioners receive a salary ?
No, the compensation is entirely honorary.
How many of these commissioners are appointed by the government, and how many by the city ?

As the law stands now there are four commis-

sioners, of whom three are appointed by the Governor in Council during pleasure, and one is appointed from time to time by the corporation of the city of Ottawa. This proposal is to add four, all of whom will be appointed by the Governor in Council.
That is to say, seven will be appointed by the Governor in Council and one by the city.
Yes.

Is it found desirable to have an even number of commissioners rather than an odd number ? Or would there be any objection to having another representative for the city ? You are doubling the number, but you are altering the proportion.

I may say when the matter was first broached I had contemplated a larger measure which would include an additional representative for the city of Ottawa, but owing to the late period of the session I concluded it was better not to do that at present. I do not think the city has any reason to complain or are complaining. Whatever is done is done entirely for the city of Ottawa. If this were a case of a joint expenditure, part of which was to be spent in Ottawa and a part somewhere else, it would be important to have the city proportionately represented. But as the whole expenditure is in Ottawa and for the benefit of Ottawa, I think the ordinary rules of proportion are not necessary to be maintained. I do not think there is any difficulty on the part of the city, and I hope next year we will be able to enlarge the scope of the Bill and give the city further representation.

If the city acquiesces I have not a word to say. But it occurred to me that the proportion fixed last year must have been based on some principle, and that if you doubled the number of commissioners it would be only fair to do it in the same proportion.

I would not be justified in saying the city has acquiesced, because there has been no formal correspondence on the subject. But I have found no objection on the part of the city, and do not anticipate any.
I suppose the money is furnished entirely by the government ?
Yes.

The city does not contribute directly. But there was an understanding between the city and the government as respects the sum of $15,000 per annum which the government were paying into the ci,ty funds for certain purposes, and it was agreed that that sum, Instead of being paid into the city funds, should be diverted into the fund of tnis
commission, and in that sense it may be said they are contributing. But the whole of the money is paid by the Dominion government.
Will the chairman have the same rights on this commission as lie had on the old ? He had two votes.
There will be no change in that respect, we have not touched that point at all, I anticipate that with the large number of the commission there will be no difficulty of that nature.
What proportion is made in the original Bill for changing the commissioners ? Do they hold office during pleasure ?
The commissioners appointed by the Governor in Council hold office during pleasure, but the commissioner of the city of Ottawa is appointed by the corporation for a term not exceeding three years.

I expected to be able to verify a statement I made the other night because I have reason to believe it is correct, but the party from whom I expected to get information is not in the city, and therefore I could not see him so as to be able to verify the statement I made, otherwise I would probably do so on this occasion. I think this arrangement will help to tide over the difficulty the commission has experienced in the past. It can be readily seen that were there only four commissioners, one of whom was chairman, and another of the commissioners did not wish to act, or could not act, only two commissioners were really left to do the work. Now, the chairman had two votes, or in case of a tie the chairman had one additional vote and he could give it to either one side or the other, he had a double voting power. At different times it was found the commission was unworkable as constituted under the old law. Ry the enlargement of the number it may be that difficulty will be largely avoided. But it seems to me that unless that commission do their work more creditably in the future than they have been doing it in the past we ought to take an early opportunity of exercising more supervision over them than we have done up to the present time.

I have heard the suggestion from some source that it would be better to have an odd number of commissioners for reasons which have been mentioned. Possibly the difficulty of a tie may be removed by the increased number, owing to the improbability that all will attend. I do not know about that. But I have heard that suggestion made and I bring it to the attention of the hon. gentleman.

I think the point may be worthy of consideration

another year. I quite anticipate that another session we will have still further legislation on this subject, but at present I have no reason to doubt that the matter will be improved to some extent by the larger number of the commission. In saying that I do not wish to be understood as assenting to all the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has said regarding the work of the commission. I think he has been misinformed-of course he received his information In good faith. My information is that the work of the commission on the whole has been very well done indeed. These gentlemen have given a great deal of time and have rendered very valuable service to the city.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

House in committee on Bill (No. 165) respecting the coasting trade of Canada.-The Minister of Justice.
On section 1,

This is a re-enactment of the law as it is now, except that the second paragraph contains a definition of the words ' coasting trade.'
On section 2,
speakername: The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick).

speechtext:
I desire to move an amendment to this clause, adding the following words after the word * ship ' in the second paragraph :
Provided, that the provisions of this section shall not apply to any foreign-built British ship that has been registered a3 a British ship prior to the 1st day of December, 1902.

I want to ask the hon. minister who has charge of this Bill in regard to the provisions imposing restrictions upon British-built vessels engaging in the coasting trade whether any corresponding restrictions exist in the British navigation laws in regard to Canadian-built vessels.
No.

Why should we introduce this discrimination against ships of British register engaging in the Canadian coasting business when we have for our own tonnage the free use of the British coasting trade in all parts of the Britsli Empire ?
This Bill is applicable not to a British-built ship but to a foreign-built ship registered in England.
A British-built vessel is not excluded by it ?
No.

Then, in regard to subsection 2 or section 2, I desire to ask Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
the hon. minister whether that does not make a change in the.rate of duty hitherto imposed ?
The rate of duty heretofore imposed was 10 per cent ad valorem on the hull of the vessel, and 25 per cent ad valorem on the hull, rigging, machinery, boiler, furniture and appurtenances of the ship.

Having in view the desirability of encouraging the increase of the Canadian marine, I should question very much whether an increase of duty from 10 to 25 per cent on foreign-built vessels that sought admission to Canadian register is a course to be pursued which is likely to be in the interests of the country. It strikes me that 10 per cent on the hull of a vessel for duty is high enough.

The first section contains a definition of the coasting laws, and it is not very important. It is in respect to section 2 that there is a departure. That requires that a foreign-built British ship, to engage in the coasting trade of Canada, shall be obliged to take out a license for which 25 per cent ad valorem of the vessel will be charged.
This will not have an ex post facto effect will it ?
No, not in regard to any vessel in Canada.

I understand you have an action now going on in the court in which the contention of your department is that a vessel bought in the United States which had got British register and came over here bad no right to engage in the coasting business ?

That was not quite the question. The question was whether or not a vessel which went to the United States and came in here under the operation of the British Consul's certificate at Chicago was entered to engage in the. coasting trade. It was held in the lower court and in the Exchequer Court that our contention was wrong, but fortunately there is such a thing as a Supreme Court in this country, and we succeeded a few days ago in getting a judgment reversing the judgment of the Exchequer Court
The judgment is that foreign-built vessels taking out a consul's certificate for the purpose of being admitted to Canadian register cannot obtain that register without paying.
No. That is the law which we have now without this amendment.
The judgment of the Exchequer Court is reversed ?
The judg-i ment of the Exchequer Court is reversed.
I would like to ask tlie liou. minister whether there is any imperial sanction required in regard to these proposed changes ?

It is provided that this Bill shall not come into force until such time as it receives the imperial sanction. The ninth paragraph says :
This Act shall not come into force until His Majesty's pleasure thereon has been signified.
That is in connection with the Merchants' Shipping Act of 1894, section 736.
Is His Majesty's pleasure signified through an imperial Act, or would it mean His Majesty's pleasure signified through a Canadian Act of parliament ?

The Merchants' Shipping Act of 1894 provides that:
The legislature of a British possession, may, by any Act or ordinance, regulate the coasting trade of that British possession, subject in every case to the following conditions :
(a) The Act or ordinance shall contain a suspending clause providing that the Act or ordinance shall not come into operation until Her Majesty's pleasure thereon has been publicly signified in the British possession in which it has been passed.
It Is to 'meet the provision of the imperial Act that we have inserted section 9 of this Bill.

The question which occurred to me was whether the language used here might mean His Majesty's pleasure signified on the advice of the government of Canada. It is a very proper provision, but I want to be sure that we are expressing it in the way that the hon. minister intended.

(Translation.) I deem it my duty to call the attention of the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) to the difference existing between our legislation respecting the coasting trade and the legislation in force in the United States. Prior to 1898, we had no passenger steamboats at St. John. At that time excursions from Canada to the United States were organized by American companies, and steamboats used to call at St. John and Iberville, at Sabrevois and l'lle aux Noix and carried passengers to Bur-



lington or Platsburg, without the government having ever interfered. The American coasting laws were then similar to the Canadian laws; but in 1898, a statute was passed by the American Congress, which reads as follows
No goods or passengers shall be carried by water, from one port of the United States to another, except in American ships, ' either directly or via a foreign port,' or for any part of the voyage.
About 1900, the people of St. John organized a transportation company, the Richelieu Navigation Company, which undertook to carry passengers and excursionists from the United States to Canada and from Canada to the United States, as had been done so far by American vessels. But the United States government soon interfered, and in the course of the last season a steamboat of the company, the 'Majestic' was seized by the American authorities. The American government Claimed the sum of twenty thousand dollars, because the navigation laws in the United States are much more drastic than ours are, the penalty being $20 for each passenger, whereas, under our legislation, the penalty amounts only to $400 in all. As the 'Majestic' was not worth $20,000. the American authorities felt inclined to enter into negotiations, and owing to the good offices of Mr. Myers, of Rouse's Point, the company succeeded in making an arrangement through which it got out of trouble by paying a fine of $200. I think it desirable that our legislation should be amended in the direction of the American law.

That is a very serious question and it was canvassed and discussed before this Bill was submitted. We launched the Bill on the assumption that we were dealing with this matter constitutionally.

There is also another consideration about it, which is, that apparently even if a foreign-built ship desired to engage in the coasting trade for only a limited period, nevertheless it would have to pay the full amount of duties.
It is really a tax on foreign ships coming in.

It is really the imposition of a duty on foreign-built ships brought into Canada for the purpose of doing a coasting trade, even if they should he employed in that trade for only a very limited period.
We impose a tax if they come in as foreign-built ships, but if they go out and get a British

register and come back again they defeat the provisions of our customs law.
